doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Writing as a parallel life and documenting visiting musicians
summary: Writing was never a living; he and others interviewed visiting Americans, and Darensbourg's 1962 interview in Jazz Monthly began their book.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Yeah. You got to a point where you actually could make a living as a writer?

Naah. No. The writing has always been a parallel thing. I mean I got married when I was 24, we started to have our family. There’s very few people in England, I can think of a couple of writers, in a sense, who said I’m going to be a full time and professional jazz writer. They were a rare breed. Max was on the Melody Maker. Okay? That was a full time job. He was very much the exception. Most of us were, I supposed, amateurs in the strict sense of the word, wanting to do things to document the music, interviewing musicians. I began to think every black person that walked up and down Oxford Street must be potentially a jazz musician you know. So if players came to town, people like me would swoop on them and try and get them to give us their stories. Because we wanted to document the music. Document the stories. I think probably by then one of the books that had interested me curiously was Hear Me Talking to Ya, you know the wonderful oral history. You know you thought God I want to do that. I want to get these stories before they all disappear you know.
Were you perhaps one of the first people to hit on some of these guys for stories do you think? Because nowadays a lot of them have been telling their stories a lot.

Well I can certainly recall, I mean I brought the book I wrote about Joe Darensbourg. That started, and that may be worth talking about for a minute or two, I saw his address in Leonard Feather’s own Encyclopedia of Jazz. So I wrote to him. You know, “Dear Joe, I’m an admirer of your music.” And we struck up a correspondence. He came to London in about 1962, just after I got married, with Louis Armstrong’s All-Stars. I interviewed him, that was the first time a full account of his career had ever appeared. That was in “Jazz Monthly.” Ultimately that led to this. So I was, with some others, there was a wonderful writer called Valerie Wilmer who is still very, very active. A number of us I think were starting out with the idea of interviewing as many visiting American

musicians as we could get to. Not necessarily the big stars, but sometimes the piano player and the bass player, rather than the top soloist perhaps. Because you’re right, obviously some of those have been interviewed extensively already. And I think that was quite a useful thing to do, enough of them was talking clearly for the first time in that sense. You know it was the first they’d been prompted to give their stories.
